blocks.p: Once you can recognize [Impulses](piece:impulses), here is what to do with them: five methods that primarily support Conscious Behavioral Action. They provide practical, accessible ways to use Impulses. These methods are especially important during Received Self-Regulation, when Impulses surface with greater clarity and your body's self-regulatory wisdom guides the process. You may use these methods any time you practice, but they reach their full potential when your thinking and your body are in sync and your body is ready to show you what it needs.
The Methods are:

None is better than another. They're simply options. Some require space to move. Some work when you're sitting still. Some need materials; others need only your mind. Your Impulse, your Polyvagal state, and what's available to you will guide which method to use.

As with all unstucking practices, maintaining your safety anchoring is the priority when using these methods. If you lose your safety anchoring while engaging with an Impulse through any of these methods, pause, re-anchor, and return when ready. These methods facilitate self-regulation only when practiced within safety.
As you read each method, notice what pulls you in. That pull is information toward self-regulation. Trust it.

Movement, as an unstucking method, is not exercise. It is not a technique for burning off excess energy or for distracting yourself from difficult feelings. Movement is a channel through which your body's impulses can be expressed and completed, thereby opening further self-regulation.

The connection between Impulse and movement is fundamental to trauma relief. Self-regulation Impulses come from incomplete actions, suspended in your nervous system. When a threat overwhelms your capacity to respond, the action your body prepared remains stuck as potential energy. Self-regulation occurs when that potential energy finds release. You mindfully engage the Impulse, allow it to move through your body, and the nervous system completes what was left unfinished. (See [Impulses](piece:impulses) for state-specific Impulse types.)

Movement potential varies. Not everyone can run. Not everyone can bend, lift, or twist. Injury, disability, chronic pain, and countless other factors shape what your body can do. Work within your movement potential, not against it. The [movement sizes](piece:anchor-movement-body-breath#movement-sizes) (small, medium, and large) provide a starting framework. If large movements like running or pushing feel inaccessible, smaller movements can achieve the same self-regulatory effect. The magnitude of the action matters less than the quality of your engagement with it. A mindful flex and release can be highly effective when done with full attention and presence.

One state requires particular care: freeze. When the dorsal vagal component of freeze eases, the frozen sympathetic emerges, potentially into an Impulse. This energy must be approached slowly. Moving too quickly or forcefully can overwhelm your system and drive you back into immobilization. Stay connected to the four signs that indicate when to pause (intolerable distress, curiosity becomes evaluation, losing connection with breath, intrusive cognitions).

Deliberate slowness helps you stay anchored in safety as the energy moves. It keeps your conscious awareness connected to the physical experience rather than letting it sweep you away. You remain in control, guiding the thaw from your safety state, allowing completion to unfold at a pace your nervous system can integrate.

Throughout any movement method, your focus belongs on the experience, not the outcome. You are not trying to achieve a certain distance, lift a certain weight, or perform a movement perfectly. Use movement to connect with and release the Impulse within you. There is no prescriptive movement; no correct way to move.

Bring your attention to the Sensations: the contact of your feet with the ground, the tension in your muscles, the spontaneous rhythm of your breath, and the heat building in your body. These Sensations are the substance of self-regulation. The external action is simply the form through which the internal experience unfolds. Stay anchored in safety, allow the defensive activation, and let the movement be the avenue through which your body completes what has been stuck.

blocks.why: Movement as an unstucking method starts from safety. This practice anchors you through movement.

blocks.p: Fidgeting is a form of small, contained movement that channels an Impulse through sensory engagement. While movements like running or pushing require space and physical capacity, fidgeting requires neither. It works when you're seated, in public spaces, and when large movements aren't accessible or appropriate. Fidgeting pairs physical action with sensory focus, like the texture of an object, the resistance it provides, the rhythm of repetitive motion.

Fidgeting facilitates self-regulation by giving your hands, and through them, your nervous system, something to do with its activation. The Impulse to squeeze, pull, twist, or stroke finds expression through the object you're holding.

But fidgeting is not merely a distraction. When done mindfully, it becomes a focal point for your attention. Pay attention to the sensory experience of fidgeting, like the slight friction of a pencil eraser on your palm or the subtle sound of caressing a favorite blanket. These sensory details anchor you in the present moment while also allowing the Impulse to discharge through small, deliberate actions.

Different states gravitate toward distinct fidgeting patterns. Flight activation often pulls toward soothing or processing-oriented fidgets: Rubik's Cubes, puzzles, soft textures, and objects that allow repetitive manipulation. These fidgets provide something to focus on as restless energy moves through small hand movements. They are calming yet still allow the experience of flight energy. However, fidgeting alone may not fully discharge flight activation. Pairing fidgets with other methods, such as flexing and releasing, often proves more effective for flight-driven impulses.

Fight activation seeks resistance. The impulse to squeeze, pull, or twist leads to durable objects: stress balls, rubber rings, anything that can withstand force. Spiked rubber rings, for instance, engage the muscles of the hands, arms, and shoulders, allowing aggressive energy to channel through pulling and squeezing motions. The key is finding objects that provide enough resistance to match the intensity of the fight impulse.

Shutdown fidgeting is minimal and sensory. In a shutdown-dominant system, there is little energy available for movement. Fidgeting may involve simply holding an object or engaging in slow, repetitive motions, such as stroking a textured surface or rolling something between your fingers. (I recommend focusing on your shutdown fidgeting while in a low-stimulation environment.)

Freeze fidgeting depends on the flavor of the freeze state. If your freeze carries more flight, the fidget might be soothing and processing-oriented. If it carries more fight energy, it might involve squeezing or pulling. As the immobility of freeze thaws under the influence of safety, the underlying activation becomes available for discharge, and the fidgeting pattern will reflect that emerging energy.

You don't need to buy specialized fidget tools. Household items work just as well: towels you can twist or squeeze, the arm of a chair, clothing you can pull, and paper towel rolls you can compress and release. The object itself matters less than how you engage with it. A rolled-up towel can provide the same resistance as an expensive stress ball. A rubber band, a piece of fabric, or a small stone: all can serve as channels for impulse expression when used mindfully. You likely have things lying around you've already purchased, like an elastic band or light weights. It might be time to dust them off.

Choose something that matches the sensory and resistance needs of your current state. Then bring your full attention to the experience: the texture, the temperature, the way your muscles engage, and the rhythm of your movements. That mindful attention transforms a simple object into a channel for self-regulation.

Creation offers a unique avenue for self-regulation: it externalizes internal experience. When you draw, paint, sculpt, or engage with any creative medium, you're translating what exists inside your body into something outside of it. This is not art-making for an audience. You're not intentionally producing something beautiful, impressive, or worthy of display. Creation, as an unstucking method, is purely about channeling your State's needs.

The connection between Impulse and creation lies in how state shapes expression. Story follows state, and so does every mark you make, every stroke, every color choice, every rhythm of movement. When you create from flight activation, your hand might move quickly, erratically, with sharp lines and restless energy. When you create from fight activation, the pressure intensifies: bold marks, forceful strokes, the medium pressed hard against the surface. Shutdown creation is slow, faint, and minimal. Freeze creation might oscillate between immobility and sudden bursts of movement. You are not trying to draw these states. You are allowing your State to flow through the creative act. The medium captures what your body is experiencing in real time.

Your creative tools are extensions of your body. A pencil, a brush, a piece of charcoal: these are not just instruments for making marks on paper. They are channels through which your internal experience can emerge. Think of them as you would your hands when fidgeting: they give form to what is formless and make visible what is felt but unseen. The canvas or paper is not a destination for a finished product. It is a surface that receives what you're releasing. You feel the impulses and sensations inside, and you let them move through your hand, through the tool, onto the page.

The practice is simple but requires letting go of the outcome. You do not need to know what you're drawing. You do not need a plan, a subject, or a goal. You anchor in safety, connect with your internal experience through the Skills Sequence, and then allow your hand to move. Scribbling works. Abstract marks work. Colors without form work. The speed of your hand, the pressure you apply, and the rhythm of the movement: all of this follows your state. If your body feels tense, you might scribble quickly and in a jittery way. If your body feels heavy, your marks might be slow and faint. Let the creative act mirror what you're feeling without trying to control it.

Creation works across States, skill levels, and media. You do not need to be an artist. You do not need training or talent. You need the willingness to let what's inside come out without judgment. Crayons, pens, markers, paint, clay, even just a pencil and scrap paper: any of these can serve. The medium matters less than your engagement with it.

Focus on the experience: the sensory experience of the creative tool in your hand, the sound it makes on the surface, the visual feedback as marks appear, and the way your body feels as you move. This sensory engagement keeps you present and anchored as the impulse discharges through the creative act. The outcome is simply evidence that the process occurred, not the intention.

Journaling is not diary-keeping, for our purposes. It is not about documenting events, organizing thoughts, or creating coherent narratives. Journaling for self-regulation is the act of channeling your internal experience through language onto a page. Words become the medium through which Sensations, Impulses, Emotions, and Cognitions find expression. The page receives what you're releasing, just as a canvas receives marks during creation.

The language of your journaling does not need to be any specific thing. Write in a structured way if you like. Fragmented, linear, bulleted, eloquent, or scattered are all fine, too. Do what feels best in that moment, guided by your underlying Impulse.

Story follows State, and so does every word you choose, every sentence structure, and every punctuation mark or lack thereof. Your State shapes not only what you write but also how you write it. Flight activation might produce rapid, stream-of-consciousness writing with incomplete thoughts racing across the page. Fight activation might show up as forceful words, all-caps, sharp punctuation, and language that pushes and resists. Shutdown writing tends toward slow, sparse entries: short sentences, long pauses, and words that barely make it onto the page. Freeze writing may oscillate between immobility (staring at a blank page) and sudden bursts of expression as immobilization begins to thaw. You are not writing about your State as an observer describing it from a distance. You are writing from within your State, allowing it to shape the writing itself.

Journaling is an unstucking method because it externalizes what is internal. The experience moves from inside your body onto the page. This doesn't mean the experience disappears. It means your relationship to it shifts. You can witness what was previously only felt. The act of writing also engages your conscious mind in alignment with your body's experience rather than in opposition to it. You're not writing to fix, solve, or eliminate what you're feeling. You're writing to give it form, to let it exist outside the confines of your nervous system.

The practice requires letting go of polish. You are not writing for an audience. You are not crafting sentences for clarity or impact. You are allowing words to spill onto the page in whatever form they take. Spelling doesn't matter. Grammar doesn't matter. Legibility doesn't matter.

Speed and intensity matter. They reflect your State. If your body feels activated, let your hand move quickly. Write without lifting the pen. Don't pause to think. If your body feels heavy or slow, let the writing be slow. Write one word at a time if that's what emerges. Maybe one letter. The rhythm of your writing should match the rhythm of your internal experience.

Doodling or sketching can accompany journaling, especially when words feel inadequate or inaccessible. A scribble in the margin, abstract shapes between sentences, lines that follow the movement of your hand: these visual elements add another dimension to the release. They allow the Impulse to flow through both language and mark-making. Some States may pull you toward words more. Others may pull you toward images. Let the balance shift as needed.

Journaling also accommodates different levels of engagement, depending on your capacity in the moment. You can write about your immediate environment: the chair you're sitting on, the texture of the paper, the sound of the pen. If you have more capacity, you can write directly into the experience: describing Sensations, naming Emotions, and following the thread of an Impulse as it moves through your body.

Throughout and no matter the words on the page, your focus belongs to the experience of writing, not to the content produced. Notice the sensation of the pen in your hand, the sound it makes on paper, the movement of your wrist and fingers, and the way your breath shifts as certain words appear. These sensory details anchor you in the present moment while the writing channels your state.

Like creativity, the journal entry, the words on the page, is evidence that the process occurred. It is not a product to be judged or revised. It is the residue of your internal experience taking external form. That process, not the result, is where self-regulation occurs.

Imagination is the most challenging and demanding of the unstucking methods. It requires sustaining detailed mental imagery while simultaneously tracking your body's response to that imagery. It also requires clarity about the distinction between imagination and reality. When used skillfully, imagination can facilitate self-regulation in ways the other methods cannot. It removes physical limitations, creates safe scenarios for Impulse expression, and allows you to rehearse completion without external action. But it is not for everyone, nor for every moment. Assess your capacity honestly before engaging this method.

Imagination serves as an unstucking method because your body responds to mental imagery as if it were real. This is not metaphorical. When you vividly imagine running, your nervous system activates the same pathways it would if you were physically running. Your heart rate may change. Your breathing may shift. The muscles involved in the imagined action may subtly engage. This phenomenon underlies why [imagining a safe place](piece:recognize-polyvagal-safety#using-your-imagination-to-explore-safety) can anchor you in a safety state.

The imagery comes first; the body follows. The same applies when using imagination to engage Impulses. If you can truly experience the details of what you're imagining, the Sensation, the movement, the environment, your body may align with your brain's processes, enabling self-regulation.
There are two ways to use imagination with Impulses:

Use imagination as an avenue for the Impulse. You identify the Impulse through the Skills Sequence, then you imagine acting on it fully, without limitation. If the impulse is to run, you imagine running: feet pounding, breath quickening, distance increasing. If the impulse is to push, you imagine pushing with full force against resistance. If the impulse is to lift, you imagine lifting. The imagination becomes the channel through which the Impulse discharges. Your body experiences the release as you remain still, mindfully tracking the Sensations, trembling, or shifts that occur in response to the imagined action.

Use imagination as an entry point to access the Impulse. You anchor in safety through an imagined scene, then allow defense to emerge within that scene. As your State shifts, the imagery shifts. A dark pond appears in the meadow. A shadow moves across the room. The details of the imagined scene reflect your State because story follows state. By mindfully witnessing these changes in your imagination, you access the Impulse or Sensation connected to the defensive state. Once accessed, you can continue working within the imagination, or you can shift to one of the other unstucking methods.
I'll share two examples of clients who used their imagination. As you will see, this unstucking method leans more heavily toward Spontaneous Expression.

Dolores used her imagination to follow her impulse. She arrived at the session with intense anxiety stemming from a dysregulated flight state. Through co-regulation with me and A->W->E, she identified an Impulse to run. She also identified a safe place: her Grandma's house. Her Grandma had been her one safe person in life, and though Grandma had passed, the memory of her house remained a powerful safety anchor.

When Dolores felt the Impulse to run, she imagined running to Grandma's house. She imagined her feet pounding on the concrete, moving away from danger and toward safety. As she held this image in her mind, her body responded. She shook and trembled, releasing stuck flight energy that had been frozen in her system.

After this spontaneous expression, she arrived at the house, stood in the doorway, and walked inside. She noticed details she had forgotten: the oversized remote, the familiar couch, the stack of magazines. She felt a connection with her Grandma, an experience now possible after using the flight Impulse.

Mildred used her imagination differently. She used it as an entry point. She began by anchoring herself in an imagined safety space: an endless green meadow with animals, flowers, and a willow tree where she could sit and breathe calmly. As she rested in this imagined safety, her body generated an Impulse to explore her freeze state. She followed that Impulse while remaining anchored in the meadow. The scene shifted.

A black pond appeared: dark, deep, and endless. Mildred did not want to enter it, but she allowed herself to notice it. She also noticed apprehension rising, which she recognized as connected to her freeze. Her imagined self curled up beneath the willow tree, bracing. In her real body, she felt the Impulse to brace. She allowed it, experienced it mindfully, and the intensity softened. The freeze began to thaw. The black pond remained in the scene, no longer a source of apprehension but simply an aspect of the meadow she could return to when ready.

This approach requires high distress tolerance and mindfulness skills. You're immobile while directly experiencing autonomic shifts. It is not easy and will likely involve intense sensations and unexpected trembles as the system shifts. Gauge your capacity honestly before using this unstucking method.

To use your imagination effectively, you must first anchor in safety. Then, as you move through the Skills Sequence, allow an image to arise. Do not force it. If no image emerges, this method is not available to you in that moment. Let it go and use one of the other methods instead. If an image arises, follow it.

Immerse yourself in sensory details: What do you see? What do you hear? What textures or temperatures are present? Let the scene unfold without directing it. Story follows state, so whatever emerges will reflect what is happening inside your nervous system. If you can mindfully experience what you're imagining, you are mindfully experiencing your State. Your body will respond, and self-regulation will occur through that response.

A necessary caution: imaginative scenes are cognitive tools: spontaneous constructs your mind creates while in your safety state to help you access your internal experience. Do not take them beyond that purpose. They are not psychological entities with independent existence. They do not need naming, dialogue, or management.

Unlike therapeutic frameworks that attempt to impose specific imagery or concepts, I recommend that you let your imagination guide you. As long as you are in your safety state, imaginative cognitions arise from your unique life experience and can serve your self-regulatory needs. Use your imagination to increase access to your inner world. Ground yourself in safety, allow defenses to surface, and let your imagination reflect what emerges. The imagination is a tool, not a reality. It serves self-regulation, and when that purpose is complete, you return fully to the present moment.

As I am sure you can see, the five unstucking methods do not exist in isolation. They are a result of the skills before them, like [Balancing and Pendulating](piece:balancing-and-pendulating). And the work you put into [building your safety state](piece:safety-cues-and-anchors). And a [new understanding of yourself](piece:stuck-not-broken).

Unstucking is not as simple as using one of the five unstucking methods. You can't skip ahead, even though you may have been taught that you just need to do x, y, or z to heal your trauma. Movement, fidgeting, creation, journaling, and imagination are only as useful as the work you put in well before this point.
"I don't know which method to use when."
There is no right or wrong. When you meditate deeply enough, your body will tell you.
"I tried a method, and nothing happened."
The unstucking methods are only useful if a genuine Impulse has surfaced through the Skills Sequence.
"Movement feels too activating."
Ensure you're well-anchored and a genuine Impulse is within you to get the most benefit from movement. Otherwise, try one of the other methods.
"Fidgeting feels like a distraction, not self-regulation."
Fidgeting becomes self-regulation only when you bring mindful awareness to it.
"Creation feels stupid. I'm just scribbling."
Arguably, the stupider it looks, the more likely you're doing it correctly (not performing, not creating for an audience). Redirect your focus to the experience, not the outcome.
"Journaling turns into rumination or trauma narratives."
You've lost safety anchoring and intrusive cognitions are a sign it's time to stop. Focus on shorter writing and focus only on the present moment.
"Imaginative Cognitions feel too complicated."
It's not easy. Focus on the other four for now.
"Can I use multiple methods in one session?"
Sure!

Acknowledge a mild defensive emotion you're carrying with you right now, like annoyance at work or frustration with your children. Pick one of the unstucking methods while letting yourself feel the emotion and use it.
This light practice serves as a simple gateway to deeper work with Impulses and using the unstucking methods. Just be open to the experience.
Before practicing:

ul: What Impulses do you think you're holding onto? What unstucking method do they want?
When you're collapsed, what does your system want? How about when you're mobilized? Or ready to connect?

blocks.p: After practicing:

ul: Was this emotion too difficult or easy?
